32379: Shamgar son of Anath is mentioned in one verse as a deliverer who killed six hundred Philistines with an ox goad. He is not called a judge, and his name and his father's name (Anath was a Canaanite goddess) suggest he may not have been an Israelite. Deborah's song places him in a time when roads were unsafe. He shows God using an unlikely person and an ordinary farm tool.
32380: Son of Anath. After Ehud, he killed six hundred Philistines with an ox goad and delivered Israel. Deborah's song mentions his days as a time of danger.
32382: 'Son of Anath' may mean he came from Beth-anath, or that he was a warrior devoted to the goddess Anath, or that he was a foreign mercenary. His Israelite identity is uncertain.
32383: He is a model of using whatever is at hand for God's purposes.
32384: Terse and practical, a working man who fought with the tool in his hand.
32387: Canaanite (army of Jabin, king of Hazor)
32390: As commander for Jabin king of Canaan, living at Harosheth-hagoyim, he oppresses Israel cruelly for twenty years with nine hundred iron chariots.
32392: He gathers his chariots against Barak at Mount Tabor. God throws his army into panic; Deborah's song says the stars fought and the river Kishon swept them away.
32394: He runs on foot to the tent of Jael, whose clan is at peace with Jabin. She gives him milk, covers him, and while he sleeps drives a tent peg through his temple.
32396: Deborah's song pictures Sisera's mother at the window asking why his chariot is so slow, while her ladies imagine him dividing the spoil.
32397: Sisera was the commander of the Canaanite army of Jabin, king of Hazor, and oppressed northern Israel for twenty years with nine hundred iron chariots. Deborah and Barak led Israel against him at Mount Tabor. A sudden storm turned the river Kishon into a flood that trapped his chariots. Sisera fled on foot and was killed in his sleep by Jael. Deborah's song ends with a haunting picture of his mother waiting at the window for a son who will never come home.
32398: Commander of Jabin's army, living at Harosheth-hagoyim. He oppressed Israel twenty years, was defeated by Barak, fled to Jael's tent and was killed by her with a tent peg. 1 Samuel 12:9 and Psalm 83:9 recall his defeat.
32399: His name is not Semitic, so some suggest he was of Sea Peoples (Philistine-related) or Hurrian background, serving as a mercenary commander.
32400: The final scene with his mother humanises the enemy and shows the cost of war, while also mocking the expectation of plunder.
32401: Ezra 2:53 lists 'children of Sisera' among temple servants after the exile. A Jewish tradition says descendants of Sisera later taught Torah, but the link to this Sisera is uncertain.
32402: Proud and commanding in his chariot, then exhausted and pleading when he begs for water.
32405: worm; crimson (a dye made from a worm)
32408: After Abimelech's violent reign, Tola son of Puah, son of Dodo, of Issachar, rises to save Israel. He lives at Shamir in the hill country of Ephraim, judges twenty-three years, and is buried there.
32409: Tola is one of the 'minor judges', whose stories are told in just a few lines. From the tribe of Issachar but living in Ephraim, he led Israel for twenty-three years after the chaos of Abimelech. His name and his father's name (Puah) match the names of Issachar's own sons in Genesis 46:13, a sign that clan names repeated across generations.
32410: Son of Puah, son of Dodo, of Issachar. He arose to save Israel, lived at Shamir in Ephraim, judged twenty-three years, and was buried at Shamir.
32411: The minor judges (Tola, Jair, Ibzan, Elon, Abdon) are given in brief notes. Some scholars think they were local administrators rather than military deliverers, and that their terms may overlap.
32412: Steady and unassuming, a judge who brought quiet after violence.
32418: Jair the Gileadite judges Israel twenty-two years. He has thirty sons who ride thirty donkeys and hold thirty towns, called Havvoth-jair ('villages of Jair'). He is buried at Kamon.
32419: Jair was a judge from Gilead, east of the Jordan, who led Israel for twenty-two years. His thirty sons riding thirty donkeys and governing thirty towns picture a wealthy, settled family; riding donkeys was a mark of status. The towns called 'villages of Jair' are linked to an earlier Jair, a descendant of Manasseh, in Numbers 32:41.
32420: A Gileadite who judged Israel twenty-two years. He had thirty sons who rode thirty donkeys and had thirty towns called Havvoth-jair. He was buried at Kamon.
32422: Some think the judge Jair was a descendant of the earlier Jair son of Manasseh (Numbers 32:41; 1 Chronicles 2:22) and inherited the 'villages of Jair'. Others think Judges reuses a famous clan name.
32423: Some readers see the many sons and donkeys as a hint of growing dynasty-like power, a theme that becomes a problem later in Judges and Samuel.
32424: A prosperous patriarch of the frontier, proud of his sons and towns.
32428: Ibzan of Bethlehem judges Israel seven years. He has thirty sons and thirty daughters; he sends his daughters to marry outside his clan and brings in thirty wives from outside for his sons.
32429: Ibzan of Bethlehem judged Israel for seven years after Jephthah. He is remembered for his large family and for arranging thirty marriages outward and thirty inward, which likely built alliances across clans. Scholars debate whether his Bethlehem is the town in Judah or a smaller Bethlehem in Zebulun.
32430: Ibzan of Bethlehem judged Israel seven years. He had thirty sons and thirty daughters, arranged marriages outside his clan for all of them, and was buried at Bethlehem.
32432: Some place him in Bethlehem of Judah; many others think Bethlehem of Zebulun (Joshua 19:15) is more likely, since the minor judges around him are northern.
32433: Ibzan was Boaz, the husband of Ruth.
32434: A shrewd family man who builds peace through marriages.
32439: Elon the Zebulunite judges Israel ten years and is buried at Aijalon in the land of Zebulun.
32440: Elon from the tribe of Zebulun judged Israel for ten years. Judges records nothing else about him except his burial at Aijalon in Zebulun. Unlike the minor judges around him, no family details are given.
32441: A Zebulunite who judged Israel ten years and was buried at Aijalon in Zebulun.
32442: Quiet and reliable, remembered only for faithful service.
32448: Abdon son of Hillel the Pirathonite judges Israel eight years. He has forty sons and thirty grandsons who ride seventy donkeys. He is buried at Pirathon in the land of Ephraim.
32449: Abdon son of Hillel, from Pirathon in Ephraim, was the last of the minor judges before Samson. He judged for eight years, and his forty sons and thirty grandsons riding seventy donkeys show a wealthy and prominent family. Samuel's list of deliverers in 1 Samuel 12:11 includes a 'Bedan', whom some identify with Abdon.
32450: Son of Hillel the Pirathonite. He judged Israel eight years, had forty sons and thirty grandsons on seventy donkeys, and was buried at Pirathon in Ephraim.
32451: The 'Bedan' of 1 Samuel 12:11 may be Abdon (the names are similar in Hebrew), or Barak (as in the Greek version), or an otherwise unknown judge.
32452: A wealthy elder of Ephraim, proud of his large household.
32456: Manoah's wife is childless. The angel of the LORD tells her she will bear a son who must be a Nazirite from the womb and will begin to save Israel from the Philistines.
32457: Prays for the visitor to return
32458: Manoah asks God to send the man again to teach them how to raise the boy. The angel returns, but only repeats what he told the wife.
32460: Manoah offers a meal and asks the visitor's name. 'Why askest thou thus after my name, seeing it is secret (wonderful)?' The angel rises in the flame of the altar, and Manoah and his wife fall on their faces.
32462: Manoah panics that they have seen God. His wife reasons calmly that God would not have accepted their offering or told them all this if he meant to kill them.
32464: When grown Samson demands a Philistine wife from Timnah, Manoah and his wife protest, but go with him to arrange it. The text adds that this was 'of the LORD'.
32466: After Samson's death his family bury him in Manoah's tomb between Zorah and Eshtaol.
32467: Manoah was a Danite from Zorah and the father of Samson. His wife, who is never named, received the angel's announcement of Samson's birth. Manoah's response is earnest but a little slow: he asks for more instructions, wants the visitor's name, and panics when he realises it was the angel of the LORD. His wife's calm good sense steadies him. Later he and his wife objected to Samson marrying a Philistine, but went along with it. The story contrasts sincere but anxious faith with quiet trust.
32468: A man of Zorah of the clan of the Danites. His barren wife was told by the angel of the LORD she would bear Samson. Manoah prayed for further guidance, offered a sacrifice, saw the angel ascend in the flame, and feared death. He opposed Samson's marriage to a Philistine. Samson was buried in his tomb.
32469: The angel whose name is 'wonderful' (Hebrew pil'i) is read by many as an appearance of the pre-incarnate Christ, linking to Isaiah 9:6 'Wonderful'. Others see a created angel speaking for God.
32470: The narrator lets the unnamed wife be the more perceptive partner, a gentle reversal of expectations.
32471: Some rabbis criticised Manoah for following behind his wife (Judges 13:11), while others defended him as respectful.
32473: Desire to raise his son rightly
32474: Fearful and slow to grasp what God was doing
32475: The angel's ascent in the flame
32476: Earnest, anxious and full of questions, a careful father who wants to get it right.
32481: Steals and returns his mother's silver
32482: Micah confesses he took 1,100 pieces of silver his mother had cursed the thief over. She blesses him and has part of it made into a carved image and a cast idol.
32484: He sets up a house of gods with an ephod and household idols and makes a son his priest. 'In those days there was no king in Israel: every man did that which was right in his own eyes.'
32486: A young Levite from Bethlehem arrives looking for work. Micah hires him as priest for ten pieces of silver a year, saying, 'Now know I that the LORD will do me good.'
32488: Six hundred Danite warriors heading north take his idols and his priest. When Micah chases them, they threaten him, and he goes home with nothing.
32489: His idol set up at Dan
32490: The Danites set up Micah's image in their new city. The priest turns out to be Jonathan, a grandson of Moses, and his descendants serve there until the exile.
32491: Micah was a man from the hill country of Ephraim whose story shows how confused Israel's religion became in the time of the judges. He stole silver from his mother, gave it back, and used it to make idols for a private shrine, all while using the LORD's name. He hired a wandering Levite as his family priest, thinking this guaranteed God's blessing. The tribe of Dan then stole both his idols and his priest and set them up in their new city. The narrator's repeated comment, 'every man did that which was right in his own eyes', is the key to the story.
32492: A man of Ephraim who made a carved image and cast idol from his mother's silver, set up a shrine, hired a Levite as priest, and lost both to the Danites, who set up the idol at Dan. The priest was Jonathan son of Gershom.
32493: The story exposes religion made to suit oneself: mixing the LORD's name with idols and treating priests as hired help. It prepares for the need for a faithful king and for proper worship.
32494: Judges 18:30 in the Hebrew writes 'Manasseh' with a raised letter n, and many scholars and rabbis think scribes added it to spare Moses' name from being linked to an idolatrous grandson.
32495: Pious-sounding but self-serving, confident that the right equipment and staff will make God bless him.
32503: Gideon, who refused to be king, has seventy sons by many wives, and one more by a concubine in Shechem, whom he names Abimelech, 'my father is king'.
32505: With money from the temple of Baal-berith he hires reckless men and kills his brothers 'upon one stone'. Only the youngest, Jotham, escapes. The men of Shechem crown Abimelech king.
32507: From Mount Gerizim Jotham tells of trees seeking a king: only the useless bramble accepts. He prays that fire will come from Abimelech and Shechem and consume each other.
32509: After three years God sends an evil spirit between Abimelech and Shechem. A revolt under Gaal fails, and Abimelech razes the city, sows it with salt, and burns about a thousand people in the tower's stronghold.
32511: Attacking the tower of Thebez, he is struck on the head by an upper millstone thrown by a woman. He orders his armour-bearer to kill him so no one will say a woman killed him.
32512: Abimelech was Gideon's son by a concubine from Shechem. Although Gideon refused to be king, Abimelech seized power by murdering seventy of his half-brothers and was crowned at Shechem, Israel's first attempt at kingship. His half-brother Jotham's fable of the bramble king predicted that Abimelech and Shechem would destroy each other, and they did. After three violent years he was killed by a millstone thrown by a woman at Thebez. Judges presents him as a warning about power taken by violence.
32513: Son of Gideon (Jerubbaal) by a Shechemite concubine. He killed seventy brothers, was made king at Shechem, ruled three years, destroyed Shechem, and died at Thebez when a woman dropped a millstone on him. Judges says God repaid his wickedness.
32514: Abimelech is the anti-judge: chosen by no one but himself, saving no one, and killing his own people. His story shows what kingship looks like without God.
32516: Many read Abimelech as the bitter fruit of Gideon's later choices: his many wives, his ephod (Judges 8:27), and naming a son 'my father is king'.
32517: Ruthless energy and ability to win local backing
32522: Ambitious, smooth in persuasion and brutal in action; obsessed with his reputation to the last.
32527: She marries one of Naomi's sons. Ruth 4:10 shows Ruth married Mahlon, so Orpah's husband was Kilion.
32529: After about ten years both of Naomi's sons die.
32531: Setting out with Naomi, she is urged to go home and find a new husband. She weeps, kisses her mother-in-law and returns 'unto her people, and unto her gods', while Ruth clings to Naomi.
32532: Orpah was a Moabite woman who married Naomi's son Kilion. After both sons died, she started out for Judah with Naomi and Ruth. When Naomi urged them to go back, Orpah wept, kissed her goodbye and returned home. She did nothing wrong: she followed Naomi's own advice. Her sensible choice is the backdrop that makes Ruth's extraordinary loyalty stand out.
32533: A Moabite who married one of Elimelech's sons (Kilion). After being widowed she went part of the way with Naomi, then at Naomi's urging kissed her and went back to her people and her gods.
32535: Orpah is not a villain. She obeys Naomi and acts reasonably. The book uses her to show that Ruth's choice was free and costly.
32536: Some midrash links her name to 'back of the neck', since she turned her back on Naomi.
32537: Orpah became the ancestor of Goliath and his brothers, the giants of Gath.
32539: Affectionate and tearful, torn between love for Naomi and the security of home.
32544: During a famine in the days of the judges, Elimelech, an Ephrathite of Bethlehem, takes his wife Naomi and sons Mahlon and Kilion to live in Moab.
32546: He dies there, leaving Naomi with her two sons.
32548: Back in Bethlehem, Naomi's need to sell Elimelech's field leads to Boaz buying it as kinsman-redeemer.
32549: Elimelech, whose name means 'my God is king', was a man of Bethlehem who moved his family to Moab during a famine. He died there, and his two sons died later, leaving Naomi alone. His name is ironic in a book set when 'there was no king in Israel'. Boaz was one of his relatives, and through Boaz's redemption of his land and his family name, Elimelech's line continued.
32550: An Ephrathite from Bethlehem-judah, husband of Naomi and father of Mahlon and Kilion. He went to Moab in a famine and died there. Boaz was of his family, and redeemed his field.
32551: Some rabbis judged him harshly, saying he was a wealthy leader who abandoned his people in the famine, and that his and his sons' deaths were punishment.
32552: The text does not blame him. Many think he simply did what families did in famine, as Abraham and Jacob had done before.
32553: A worried provider, making a hard choice to keep his family alive.
32558: He moves to Moab with his parents, marries there, and dies after about ten years without children.
32560: Boaz acquires Ruth, 'the wife of Mahlon', so that the dead man's name will not be cut off from his family and town.
32561: Mahlon was the elder son of Elimelech and Naomi and Ruth's first husband. He died in Moab without children. When Boaz married Ruth, he did it in part 'to raise up the name of the dead', so that Mahlon's family line would continue through Ruth's son.
32562: Son of Elimelech and Naomi, husband of Ruth. He died in Moab. Boaz married Ruth to continue Mahlon's name.
32563: The names Mahlon and Kilion sound like 'sickness' and 'wasting away', which may be a storyteller's touch hinting at their early deaths. The meanings are not certain.
32564: Rarely heard; imagined as a gentle young man far from home.
32570: He goes to Moab with his family, marries a Moabite woman, and dies there, leaving Naomi bereft of both sons.
32572: Boaz buys from Naomi all that belonged to Elimelech, Kilion and Mahlon.
32573: Kilion was the younger son of Elimelech and Naomi. He married Orpah in Moab and died there, childless. His death, with his brother's, left Naomi empty and set the scene for the book of Ruth.
32574: Son of Elimelech and Naomi. Since Ruth was Mahlon's wife (Ruth 4:10), Orpah was Kilion's. He died in Moab; Boaz redeemed his share of the family property.
32575: Rarely heard; imagined as a young man who never made it home.
32578: Ephraim (by residence); Levite by the Chronicler's genealogy
32584: Every year he goes up from Ramah to worship and sacrifice at Shiloh, and he gives Hannah a double portion because he loves her.
32586: When Hannah weeps over her childlessness he asks, 'Am I not better to you than ten sons?' The question is tender but misses the depth of her grief.
32588: He lets Hannah keep Samuel at home until he is weaned and supports her vow to give the boy to the LORD's service.
32590: Eli blesses Elkanah and Hannah, and Hannah later bears three more sons and two daughters.
32591: Elkanah was a devout man from Ramathaim-zophim in the hill country of Ephraim and the husband of Hannah and Peninnah. He went up to Shiloh every year to worship, loved Hannah openly even though she had no children, and backed her vow to dedicate their son Samuel to the LORD. He is a quiet, faithful figure in a dark period when Eli's sons were corrupting the sanctuary. The text calls him an Ephraimite, but 1 Chronicles lists him in a Levite family line; both can be true if 'Ephraimite' describes where he lived rather than his tribe.
32592: Son of Jeroham, from Ramathaim-zophim in Ephraim, with two wives, Hannah and Peninnah (1 Sam 1:1-2). Worshipped yearly at Shiloh (1 Sam 1:3). Loved Hannah and gave her a double portion (1 Sam 1:5). Supported her vow (1 Sam 1:23). Listed among the Levites, descendants of Kohath (1 Chr 6:27).
32593: Rabbinic tradition remembers him as a man who encouraged others to make the pilgrimage to Shiloh, taking a different route each year so more people would join. This is legend, not text.
32594: Many scholars see the Levite genealogy in Chronicles as a later way of explaining why Samuel, a non-priest, could serve at the sanctuary; others take it as historical and read 'Ephraimite' as a geographical label (debated).
32595: Gentle, steady and a little puzzled by his wife's sorrow; speaks plainly and kindly, as a man trying to make things right at home.
32601: Year after year at Shiloh she taunts Hannah for being childless until Hannah weeps and will not eat.
32602: Peninnah was Elkanah's second wife, who had children while Hannah had none. The text calls her Hannah's 'rival' and says she provoked her bitterly every year at the festival. Her story echoes the earlier tension between Sarah and Hagar and between Rachel and Leah.
32603: Had children while Hannah had none (1 Sam 1:2). Called Hannah's rival, she provoked her to irritate her, year after year (1 Sam 1:6-7).
32604: Some rabbis claim she taunted Hannah to push her to pray harder; this softens her character but has no basis in the text.
32605: Sharp-tongued and proud of her children; speaks with barbs dressed up as remarks.
32608: Earlier chronology of the judges period
32611: With his brother he takes the best meat by force before the fat is offered to God and sleeps with women serving at the tent entrance. He ignores his father's warning.
32612: Dies when the ark is captured
32613: He carries the ark into battle against the Philistines as if it were a lucky charm. Israel is routed, the ark is taken, and Hophni and Phinehas are killed on the same day, as foretold.
32614: Hophni was the elder son of the priest Eli. The text calls him and his brother 'worthless men' who 'did not know the LORD', because they stole from the sacrifices and abused their office. Both died on one day in battle against the Philistines, the sign a man of God had given Eli.
32615: Priest at Shiloh with his brother (1 Sam 1:3). Took meat by force and treated the LORD's offering with contempt (1 Sam 2:12-17). Refused to listen to Eli (1 Sam 2:25). His death with his brother foretold (1 Sam 2:34) and fulfilled at Ebenezer/Aphek (1 Sam 4:11).
32616: Entitled and dismissive; talks about holy things as if they were perks of the job.
32620: Together with Hophni he seizes sacrificial meat and sins with the women who served at the sanctuary.
32622: He dies when the ark is captured. On hearing the news his pregnant wife goes into labour, names the boy Ichabod, and dies.
32623: Phinehas was Eli's younger son and a priest at Shiloh. He shares his name with the zealous grandson of Aaron, which makes his corruption all the sharper by contrast. He died with his brother when the Philistines took the ark, and his widow named their newborn son Ichabod, 'the glory has departed'.
32624: Eli's son, priest at Shiloh (1 Sam 1:3); one of the 'worthless men' who despised the LORD's offering (1 Sam 2:12-17). Killed with Hophni (1 Sam 4:11). Father of Ichabod (1 Sam 4:19-21) and of Ahitub (1 Sam 14:3).
32625: Careless and grasping; treats warnings as an old man's fussing.
32627: Where is the glory? / No glory
